subsections.subsection_title: What the OSCE station may say

blocks.text: Typical scenarios include:
A 25-year-old woman presents with a painless lump near the vaginal opening. Take a focused history and outline management.
A 30-year-old woman presents with a painful vulval swelling and fever. Assess and manage her.
Examine a patient with a suspected Bartholin gland cyst and report your findings.
A 45-year-old woman presents with a new Bartholin-region mass. Discuss the differential diagnoses and investigations.
A woman develops a rapidly enlarging vulval swelling after childbirth. Assess her urgently.
A photograph shows a solid vulval mass. Describe the lesion and discuss the possible diagnoses.
A patient presents with multiple small vulval lumps. Discuss your differential diagnoses.
Use a respectful, structured approach.

Good morning. My name is Dr. … I understand that you have noticed a lump around your genital area. I would like to ask you some questions about when it started, whether it is painful, and whether you have experienced any other symptoms. I would then explain the examination and any tests or treatment that may be necessary. Because this is an intimate examination, I will ensure your privacy and offer a chaperone. Is that alright with you?
Before examination:
Confirm identity and obtain consent.
Explain the procedure and offer a chaperone.
Ask about pain and provide appropriate analgesia.
Ensure privacy, adequate lighting and appropriate exposure.
Use gloves and suitable infection-control precautions.
If the patient has severe pain, haemodynamic instability, fever or a rapidly expanding swelling, prioritise urgent assessment.
Ask:
When did you first notice it?
Where exactly is it located?
Did it develop suddenly or gradually?
Has it increased in size?
Is it painful, tender or itchy?
Is the pain constant or worse when walking, sitting or having intercourse?
Has it discharged pus, blood or other fluid?
Has it ulcerated or changed colour?
Have you had a similar lump before?
Has it resolved spontaneously or required drainage?
Is there more than one lump?
Clinical interpretation:
A painless, unilateral lump near the posterolateral vaginal opening suggests a Bartholin duct cyst.
A painful, red, tender swelling in the same location suggests a Bartholin abscess.
A sudden, rapidly enlarging swelling after trauma or childbirth raises concern for a vulval haematoma.
A persistent, firm or irregular mass raises concern for a solid lesion, including malignancy.
Ask about:
Fever, chills or malaise.
Difficulty walking, sitting or passing urine.
Vaginal discharge or genital ulcers.
Dysuria or other urinary symptoms.
Bleeding or spontaneous ulceration.
Lower abdominal pain if infection or another pelvic condition is suspected.
Recent childbirth, episiotomy, genital surgery, trauma or sexual intercourse.
Ask about:
Last menstrual period and pregnancy possibility.
Menopausal status.
Previous gynaecological conditions or procedures.
Previous STIs and relevant sexual exposure.
Previous Bartholin cysts or abscesses.
Recent sexual partners and STI symptoms, when clinically relevant.

content_groups.group_title: D. Medical history and risk factors

blocks.text: Ask about:
Diabetes or immunosuppression.
Medications, including anticoagulants if a haematoma is possible.
Drug allergies.
Previous vulval lesions or skin disorders.
Smoking and other relevant risk factors if malignancy is suspected.

A new Bartholin-region mass in a woman aged 40 years or older, particularly after menopause, warrants assessment to exclude malignancy. Age alone does not establish cancer, but it changes the threshold for biopsy or specialist investigation.
The first step is to distinguish a cystic or fluid-filled swelling from a solid mass, while recognising that examination alone may not always establish the diagnosis.
Usually unilateral and located at the lower posterolateral vaginal opening.
Often painless and fluctuant.
May cause discomfort during walking, sitting or intercourse if large.
Usually lacks marked surrounding inflammation unless infected.
OSCE clue: Painless lump at the 4 or 8 o'clock region.
Typically very painful, tender and swollen.
Surrounding erythema and warmth may be present.
Walking and sitting may be difficult.
Fever or systemic symptoms can occur.
OSCE clue: Tender, inflamed Bartholin-region swelling.
Usually a small, well-circumscribed dermal or subcutaneous lump.
Often painless and mobile.
May develop after trauma or surgery.
Can become inflamed or infected.
OSCE clue: Superficial, well-defined lump away from the typical Bartholin location.
May develop suddenly after childbirth, trauma or a procedure.
Can cause severe pain and tense swelling.
May be associated with bruising or significant blood loss.
A large or expanding haematoma can cause haemodynamic instability.
OSCE clue: Rapid swelling with severe pain following trauma or delivery.
Multiple papillary or cauliflower-like growths.
Usually skin-coloured or pink.
May be asymptomatic or cause irritation.
Associated with certain types of human papillomavirus (HPV).
OSCE clue: Multiple superficial papillary lesions rather than one deep cyst.
A caruncle is a small fleshy lesion at the urethral meatus, often in postmenopausal women.
Urethral prolapse appears as circumferential eversion of urethral mucosa.
Bleeding, discomfort or urinary symptoms may occur.
OSCE clue: The lesion is centred on the urethral opening, not the Bartholin region.
May present as a persistent lump, nodule, ulcer or area of thickened skin.
May be firm, irregular, fixed, pigmented or prone to bleeding.
Suspicion increases with a new or changing lesion in an older woman.
OSCE clue: Persistent, solid or atypical mass requiring specialist assessment.
Other differentials include lipoma, hidradenitis suppurativa, a vulval varicosity, an infected skin cyst, a vaginal wall cyst and, less commonly, other soft-tissue tumours.
Check:
General appearance and level of distress.
Temperature, pulse, blood pressure and other vital signs as indicated.
Signs of fever or systemic infection.
Pallor, dizziness or circulatory compromise if bleeding or a haematoma is suspected.
Ability to walk and pass urine.
A rapidly expanding swelling with severe pain or haemodynamic compromise requires urgent management rather than a prolonged routine examination.
With consent, a chaperone offered and appropriate exposure, inspect both sides of the vulva.
Assess:
Exact location of the lump.
Number and size of swellings.
Symmetry.
Skin colour and surrounding erythema.
Bruising, ulceration or discharge.
Whether the lump appears superficial or deep.
Relationship to the vaginal opening and urethral meatus.
Measure the lump in centimetres and document the anatomical site precisely.
If appropriate and tolerated, assess:

rows: Soft, cystic, fluctuant, firm or hard
Mobile or fixed to surrounding tissues
Spontaneous drainage or discharge from a duct or skin opening

blocks.text: Do not squeeze a lump to determine its contents. Avoid unnecessary manipulation of a suspected haematoma, very painful abscess or suspicious tumour.
Inspect the urethral meatus if the lesion is anterior.
Assess the vaginal introitus and posterolateral regions for a Bartholin lesion.
Inspect the perineum and perianal area if relevant.
Assess inguinal lymph nodes if malignancy or significant infection is suspected.
Explain that the examination is finished.
Help the patient cover themselves and get comfortable.
Ask about pain and answer questions.
Explain the findings and next steps.
Document the findings and consent and chaperone details according to local policy.
A speculum examination, bimanual examination or imaging is performed only if indicated by the presentation. It is not required automatically for every vulval lump.
Use a structured description: site, size, consistency, tenderness, mobility, skin changes and associated findings.

“There is a solitary, approximately 3 cm, smooth, well-circumscribed swelling in the left posterolateral aspect of the vaginal opening, corresponding to the Bartholin gland region. It is fluctuant and minimally tender, with no significant surrounding erythema or ulceration. The findings are suggestive of a Bartholin duct cyst. I would assess the impact on daily activities, check for features of infection and determine whether treatment or observation is appropriate.”

“There is a unilateral swelling in the right Bartholin gland region, approximately 4 cm in diameter, with marked tenderness, surrounding erythema and local warmth. The patient is experiencing difficulty sitting and walking. These findings suggest a Bartholin abscess. I would assess vital signs and systemic illness, provide analgesia and arrange prompt gynaecological assessment for drainage and appropriate antimicrobial treatment if indicated.”

“There is a rapidly developed, tense, painful swelling of the vulva with associated bruising following recent childbirth. The findings raise concern for a vulval haematoma. I would immediately assess haemodynamic stability, quantify bleeding, obtain appropriate intravenous access and urgent obstetric or gynaecological review.”

“There is a solitary, approximately 2 cm, firm, irregular vulval mass with an abnormal surface and reduced mobility. These findings are concerning for a solid vulval lesion, including possible malignancy. I would assess regional lymph nodes and arrange urgent specialist assessment with biopsy as indicated.”
Only describe firmness, fluctuation, tenderness or fixation if you have actually assessed those features.
Investigations depend on the suspected diagnosis. A typical uncomplicated Bartholin cyst may be diagnosed clinically, while an atypical or suspicious lump needs further assessment.

rows: When pregnancy is possible and it may affect treatment or procedures
Suspected significant bleeding, systemic infection or a large haematoma
When significant infection or systemic inflammation is suspected
If sepsis or serious systemic infection is suspected
Selected abscesses, recurrent infection or treatment failure
When sexual exposure, cervicitis or an STI is suspected
Uncertain diagnosis, suspected deep collection or haematoma, or a mass requiring further characterisation
Suspicious, persistent or atypical mass; particular consideration for a new Bartholin-region mass in women aged 40 or older
To establish the diagnosis of a biopsied or excised lesion

blocks.text: Important distinction: A Bartholin cyst is often a clinical diagnosis. Routine imaging is not necessary for every typical cyst or abscess. A new mass in an older or postmenopausal woman, however, warrants a lower threshold for biopsy or specialist assessment.
Management depends on symptoms and examination findings.
Small and asymptomatic: observation and reassurance may be appropriate.
Symptomatic or large: warm sitz baths and analgesia may provide temporary relief, but persistent or troublesome cysts may require a procedure.
Recurrent or significantly symptomatic: drainage with a Word catheter or marsupialisation may be considered.
New mass in a woman aged 40 years or older: specialist assessment to exclude malignancy, with biopsy considered as indicated.
Simple incision and drainage alone has a relatively high recurrence rate, so an appropriate procedure that maintains drainage is often preferred for symptomatic cysts or abscesses.
Management commonly involves:
Assessing the severity of pain and any systemic illness.
Providing analgesia.
Arranging drainage, commonly with a Word catheter, or another appropriate procedure.
Considering culture in selected cases, such as recurrent infection or treatment failure.
Using antibiotics when there is cellulitis, systemic illness, selected STI-related infection or another clear indication.
Antibiotics alone may not adequately treat a well-established abscess that requires drainage.
A vulval haematoma can be an emergency, especially following childbirth or trauma.
Assess airway, breathing and circulation as appropriate.
Record vital signs and establish intravenous access if significant bleeding is suspected.
Check haemoglobin, blood group and crossmatch when indicated.
Provide analgesia and urgent obstetric or gynaecological assessment.
Small, stable haematomas may be managed conservatively with close monitoring, analgesia and ice packs applied safely.
Large, expanding or unstable haematomas may require surgical evacuation, haemostasis or other specialist intervention.
Do not discharge a patient with an expanding, severely painful haematoma or signs of circulatory compromise.
Observe if small and asymptomatic.
Treat infection if present.
Consider elective excision for persistent symptoms, recurrent infection or diagnostic uncertainty.
Send excised tissue for histopathology when appropriate.
Explain that warts are usually associated with HPV and are often benign.
Options include observation, prescribed topical therapies or clinician-administered treatments such as cryotherapy or surgical removal.
Choice depends on lesion location, size, pregnancy status and patient preference.
Reconsider the diagnosis and biopsy atypical or suspicious lesions.
Assess urinary symptoms and bleeding.
Mild symptomatic caruncles may respond to appropriate conservative treatment, including topical oestrogen in selected postmenopausal patients.
Persistent bleeding, atypical lesions or diagnostic uncertainty warrant specialist assessment.
Urethral prolapse may require specialist-directed treatment, particularly if bleeding, thrombosis or urinary obstruction occurs.
Arrange urgent referral to an appropriate gynaecology or vulval specialist service.
Obtain a biopsy through the appropriate pathway.
Assess inguinal lymph nodes.
Plan further investigation and treatment according to histology and specialist assessment.
Do not simply drain or excise an atypical mass without considering whether it requires a planned diagnostic pathway.

subsections.subsection_title: Common examiner questions and model answers

blocks.text: Q1. What is a Bartholin gland cyst?

Answer: It is a cyst caused by obstruction of a Bartholin gland duct, leading to accumulation of secretions. It typically presents as a unilateral lump in the posterolateral region of the vaginal opening.
Q2. What is the difference between a Bartholin cyst and an abscess?

Answer: A cyst is often painless and fluctuant, whereas an abscess usually causes marked pain, tenderness and swelling, sometimes with erythema, fever or systemic illness. Clinical appearances can overlap.
Q3. Why is simple incision and drainage not always the preferred treatment?
Answer: The opening may close prematurely, allowing the collection to recur. A Word catheter or marsupialisation can maintain drainage and may reduce recurrence in appropriately selected patients.
Q4. When should you suspect a Bartholin gland malignancy?

Answer: Particularly when a woman aged 40 years or older, or a postmenopausal woman, develops a new Bartholin-region mass. A firm, irregular, fixed or persistent lesion also raises concern. Specialist assessment and biopsy should be considered.
Q5. What is the management of a vulval haematoma following childbirth?

Answer: Assess haemodynamic stability and bleeding immediately. Small, stable haematomas may be managed conservatively with close observation and analgesia. Expanding, large or unstable haematomas may require urgent surgical intervention and resuscitation.
Q6. What are the indications for ultrasound of a vulval lump?

Answer: Ultrasound may help when the diagnosis is uncertain, a collection or haematoma is suspected, or the extent of a deeper mass needs assessment. It is not routinely required for a typical uncomplicated Bartholin cyst.
Q7. Are antibiotics always required for a Bartholin abscess?
Answer: No. Drainage is often the main treatment. Antibiotics are considered when there is surrounding cellulitis, systemic infection, selected STI-related infection or another specific indication.
Q8. What are the differential diagnoses of a vulval lump?

Answer: Bartholin cyst or abscess, epidermal inclusion cyst, haematoma, lipoma, hidradenitis suppurativa, anogenital warts, urethral caruncle, vaginal wall cyst and benign or malignant vulval tumours.
Q9. What complications can occur with a vulval haematoma?
Answer: Severe pain, progressive swelling, urinary obstruction, significant blood loss, anaemia and haemodynamic instability.
Q10. How would you counsel a patient with a recurrent Bartholin cyst?

Answer: Explain the possibility of recurrence, discuss options such as Word catheter placement or marsupialisation, review symptoms and infection risk, and arrange appropriate follow-up. Atypical masses require reassessment rather than repeated treatment as a simple cyst.
Failing to identify the precise anatomical location of the lump.
Confusing a Bartholin cyst with a urethral lesion.
Forgetting to assess tenderness, consistency and surrounding inflammation.
Missing signs of a rapidly expanding haematoma.
Assuming every painful lump requires antibiotics alone.
Performing simple drainage without considering recurrence or the appropriate procedure.
Failing to consider malignancy in a new Bartholin-region mass in an older woman.
Ordering unnecessary investigations for a typical uncomplicated cyst.
Forgetting to obtain consent and offer a chaperone.
Failing to explain the diagnosis, treatment choices and follow-up.
Location: identify the exact site and anatomical structures involved.
Underlying consistency: cystic, fluctuant, soft, firm or hard.
Mobility and measurements: document size, borders and fixation.
Pain and associated pathology: tenderness, infection, bleeding or malignancy warning signs.
F — Fever or systemic illness.
A — Acute, rapidly expanding swelling.
S — Severe pain, significant bleeding or shock.
T — Suspicious or persistent tumour, especially in an older patient.
